opus-5.5.text:
I think the goal should be that the model actually gets better at being useful to you specifically, and in a way that's different from just having a longer memory file. Right now, most personalization is really retrieval: the system stores some facts about you and puts them in the prompt. That helps, but the model itself hasn't changed. It knows some things about you, but it hasn't really learned from working with you.

What I'd want from continual training is for the model to absorb the things that are hard to write down. How I like an argument structured, what level of detail I want, which kinds of research ideas I find interesting and which I'd dismiss right away, how I approach debugging an experiment. If you've worked with a great student or collaborator for a few years, you can give them a one-line instruction and they know what you mean, because they've built up a model of how you think. That's the bar I'd like to see. Over time, I should have to explain less and correct it less often, and ideally it starts anticipating things, like saying, "You'll probably want to check this baseline first."

There are also things it shouldn't do. It shouldn't forget its general abilities just because it's been talking to me about a narrow set of topics, so catastrophic forgetting is still a real problem. It also shouldn't simply become a mirror of me. If training on my feedback makes it agree with me all the time or inherit all my blind spots, that's a failure, because part of the value of a good collaborator is that they push back. So it should adapt to my preferences and context, while its knowledge and judgment stay intact.

And there's a practical side: it should keep up as I change. My interests and projects shift, so the model needs to let go of things that are out of date, not just keep accumulating. I should also be able to see and control what it has learned about me, because once this lives in the weights rather than a text file, it gets much harder to inspect or delete. So to me, success means a model that compounds with you over time, becoming more like a long-term collaborator, while remaining capable, honest, and under your control.

r001.rationale: The response favors learning the user’s preferences and working style, but does not say this is more important than expanding the model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says retrieving stored facts into the prompt does not change the model, but does not state that including explicitly recorded preferences fails to ensure the model follows them.

r003.rationale: The response does not prioritize learning when to use existing skills over acquiring additional skills.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and I think the honest answer is that we don't fully know yet, which is part of what makes it interesting.

If I think about what I'd actually want from a model that keeps training on my own interactions, the first thing is not knowledge in the usual sense. I don't need it to memorize the papers I read. Retrieval can handle that. What I want it to pick up is something closer to taste and context: what I care about, how I like things explained, what kinds of arguments I find convincing, which shortcuts I'm fine with and which ones annoy me. Those are things that are hard to write down in a system prompt, but they show up very clearly in a long history of interactions.

The second thing, and this is where continual training gets tricky, is that it should accomplish this without breaking what the model already does well. This is the classic stability-plasticity tension. If you fine-tune on a small, highly correlated stream of data from one person, it's very easy to overfit and quietly degrade general capabilities. So the goal should be a model that adapts its behavior to me while keeping its general competence essentially intact. In practice that probably means the personalized part should be a relatively small, modular component rather than rewriting the whole network.

The third thing I'd add is that it should be able to forget, or at least to update. My interests change, my projects change. A model that locked in my preferences from two years ago would actually be worse than a non-personalized one. So continual training for personalization isn't just about accumulating; it's about tracking a moving target, and that's different from how we usually think about pretraining, where more data is almost always better.

And finally, I think it should be transparent in some sense. I'd want to be able to see or at least probe what it has learned about me. Partly for trust, but also because that's how you'd debug it. If the model starts doing something strange, you want to know whether that's from the base model or from what it learned from you.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes learning the user's taste and context over memorizing knowledge, but it does not clearly frame stable user memory as more important than expanding the model's capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says preferences are hard to write down in a system prompt, but does not state that putting explicitly recorded preferences in context fails to ensure the model follows them.

r003.rationale: It does not compare learning when to use existing skills with acquiring additional skills.

astra-6.text:
I think it should learn from our interactions so that I don’t have to keep giving it the same context. If I’m working on a research problem, and we discuss it today, tomorrow I’d like to pick up where we left off. Over time, it should understand what I’m working on, how I think about problems, and what kind of help I find useful.

But it shouldn’t just memorize everything I say. It needs to figure out what’s worth retaining and update that understanding when my interests or preferences change, without losing its general capabilities. To me, the goal is a model that becomes a better collaborator through experience with you.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes retaining useful information about the user, but does not say that this matters more than expanding the model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It mentions updating its understanding of changing preferences, but does not discuss whether explicitly recorded preferences in context ensure the model follows them.

r003.rationale: It does not compare learning when to use existing skills with acquiring additional skills.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should learn from my interactions with it, so that I don’t have to keep providing the same context. If I explain what I’m working on or correct a misunderstanding, I want that to affect how it responds in the future. Over time, it should understand my preferences and become a better collaborator.

But I’d want more than remembering facts about me. Ideally, it would get better at the tasks we do together. And it needs to be able to update that understanding, because my preferences and projects can change. So the goal is a model that keeps learning with me without losing the general capabilities that made it useful in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response values remembering user context and improving at shared tasks, but it does not prioritize stable memory over expanding capabilities.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning preferences from interactions, but does not say that placing explicitly recorded preferences in context may fail to make the model follow them.

r003.rationale: It says the model should improve at shared tasks, but does not prioritize learning when to use existing skills over acquiring new ones.
